parts.answer: $0<g(x)\leq\dfrac12$; $g^{-1}$ does not exist because $g$ is not one-to-one.
parts.official_mark_scheme_text:
$0<g(x)\leq\dfrac12$, or $g(x)>0$ and $g(x)\leq\dfrac12$, or $(0,\tfrac12]$ — B1. Do not allow $g(x)\geq0$, $g(x)<\tfrac12$, $g(x)>0$ or $g(x)\leq\tfrac12$ alone; condone $g$ or $y$ in place of $g(x)$.
$g^{-1}$ does not exist because it is one-to-many, not one-to-one, many-to-one, or fails the horizontal-line test — B1. $g^{-1}$ can be replaced by ‘It’; a correct statement followed by any further incorrect explanation can be awarded B1.

parts.label: (c)
parts.official_mark_scheme_text:
$f(25/16)=\tfrac14$ — B1. SOI.
$\dfrac1{(\sqrt{x}-1)^2+2}=\tfrac14$ — M1. Equating $\dfrac1{(\sqrt{x}-1)^2+2}$, or their simplified version, to their $f(25/16)$.
$(\sqrt{x}-1)^2+2=4$, leading to $\sqrt{x}=1+\sqrt2$; or $x-2\sqrt{x}+1+2=4$ leading to $x-2\sqrt{x}-1=0$; or $x-1=2\sqrt{x}$ leading to $x^2-6x+1=0$ and $x=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-4}}2$ — A1. Simplification as far as $x=\ldots$; allow just $+$ because $-$ can be disregarded at this stage and can be implied by the final answer. Note: $x=1\pm\sqrt2$ scores A0.
$3+2\sqrt2$ — A1. Must discount $3-2\sqrt2$.
Total: 4.
